title: Induction
body:
The technique itself is written up in **[[Proof By Induction]]**: base case, inductive
step, strong induction, worked examples. This note exists because both names are linked
from other courses, and it holds the one distinction worth separating out.

**Ordinary induction** is indexed by a number: prove $P(1)$, then $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$.

**Structural induction** is indexed by how a recursive object is *built*: prove the
property for the base constructors, then prove it survives each way of assembling a bigger
object from smaller ones. It is the same principle (there is a well-founded ordering and
you descend it) but you never write down an $n$.

Structural is the version the computer science courses actually use, because their objects are
[[Tree]]s, [[Context-Free Grammars|derivation trees]], and recursive functions rather than
integers:

- [[Recursion]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: the base case of the function is
  the base case of the proof, and the recursive call is the inductive hypothesis.
- [[Context-Free Grammars]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: prove a property of every
  string a grammar generates by inducting over the derivation.
- [[Binary Search Tree]] and [[Tree]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: height and node-count
  claims are structural inductions over subtrees.
- [[Program Correctness]] in [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]: this is the course that uses it as its
  main tool rather than occasionally. An [[Algebraic Data Type]] hands you the case split
  directly, one case per constructor, so the data definition determines the proof's shape.
